This document runs on its own: it needs no downloaded data or helper files.
Open it in RStudio and run the chunks in order, or use **Render** to run the
whole document in a fresh session. The simulations use invented data with
known population parameters so that we can check whether an interval covers
its target. The turnout example uses rounded published summaries.

## 0. Setup

The calculations use base R. The graphs use `ggplot2`, and a few summaries
use `dplyr`, both familiar from the last two seminars.

```{r}
# Install once if needed, in the Console:
# install.packages(c("ggplot2", "dplyr"))
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

ci_colors <- c("Contains mu" = "#005a8b", "Misses mu" = "#b34b12")
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 14))
```

## 1. From the turnout difference to an interval

The Neighbors mailing group had reported turnout of 37.8%; the Civic Duty
group had 31.5%. These are the rounded figures used in Blackwell's lecture
from Gerber, Green, and Larimer (2008). A turnout indicator is 1 for a voter
and 0 otherwise, so its sample mean is the turnout proportion.

For two **independent** samples, estimate the SE of their mean difference by

$$\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\widehat D)
=\sqrt{S_Y^2/n_Y+S_X^2/n_X}.$$

Here we use the plug-in Bernoulli variance $\hat p(1-\hat p)$ with the
rounded proportions. Using sample variances instead would multiply each
variance by $n/(n-1)$, a negligible difference for these group sizes.

```{r}
p_neigh <- .378
n_neigh <- 38201
p_civic <- .315
n_civic <- 38218

estimate <- p_neigh - p_civic
se_diff <- sqrt(p_neigh * (1 - p_neigh) / n_neigh +
                p_civic * (1 - p_civic) / n_civic)
critical <- qnorm(.975)
turnout_ci <- estimate + c(-1, 1) * critical * se_diff

data.frame(estimate_pp = 100 * estimate,
           se_pp = 100 * se_diff,
           lower_pp = 100 * turnout_ci[1],
           upper_pp = 100 * turnout_ci[2])
```

Multiplying by 100 changes proportions into **percentage points**.

**Design qualification:** this is a classroom independent-samples
calculation, not a reproduction of the paper's uncertainty estimates. The
original treatment was assigned to households, so inference for that study
must respect household assignment and dependence. A formula alone does not
establish that its assumptions fit a study.

## 2. Simulate a single interval

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent draws from $N(1,10)$, where 10 is the
**variance**. R's `rnorm()` asks for the standard deviation, `sqrt(10)`.

```{r}
set.seed(2143)
mu <- 1
sigma <- sqrt(10)
n <- 500
x <- rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

estimate <- mean(x)
se <- sd(x) / sqrt(n)
critical <- qnorm(.975)
lower <- estimate - critical * se
upper <- estimate + critical * se

data.frame(estimate, se, lower, upper,
           covers = lower <= mu & mu <= upper)
```

The parameter `mu` stays fixed. Drawing another sample changes `mean(x)`,
`sd(x)`, and the two endpoints. The Normal cutoff is an approximation here
because we estimated the population SD. At $n=500$ it works very well.

## 3. Repeat the sampling process and measure coverage

`n` counts observations **within** each sample; `B` counts independent
**repetitions** of the whole experiment. We reset the seed so that the first
sample below is the same one as in Section 2.

```{r}
set.seed(2143)
mu <- 1
sigma <- sqrt(10)
n <- 500
B <- 10000
critical <- qnorm(.975)

ci <- data.frame(trial = seq_len(B),
                 estimate = rep(NA_real_, B),
                 se = rep(NA_real_, B),
                 lower = rep(NA_real_, B),
                 upper = rep(NA_real_, B))

for (i in seq_len(B)) {
  x <- rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
  ci$estimate[i] <- mean(x)
  ci$se[i] <- sd(x) / sqrt(n)
  ci$lower[i] <- ci$estimate[i] - critical * ci$se[i]
  ci$upper[i] <- ci$estimate[i] + critical * ci$se[i]
}

ci <- ci |>
  mutate(covers = lower <= mu & mu <= upper,
         result = if_else(covers, "Contains mu", "Misses mu"))

ci |>
  summarise(repetitions = n(),
            coverage = mean(covers),
            average_width = mean(upper - lower))
```

`mean(covers)` treats `TRUE` as 1 and `FALSE` as 0. It estimates
$P(L\leq\mu\leq U)$, the procedure's coverage probability.

### Plot the first 100 intervals

Each vertical segment comes from a different sample. The horizontal line
marks the same population mean in every repetition.

```{r}
first100 <- ci |> slice_head(n = 100)

ggplot(first100, aes(x = trial, y = estimate, color = result)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mu, color = "#172d42") +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), linewidth = .7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = ci_colors) +
  labs(x = "Independent sample / interval", y = "Mean and 95% interval",
       color = NULL,
       subtitle = paste(sum(first100$covers), "of these 100 intervals contain mu")) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

We should not expect exactly 95 covering intervals in every batch of 100.
The simulation also has sampling error. The SE of our estimated coverage
is approximately

$$\sqrt{\widehat p(1-\widehat p)/B}.$$

```{r}
coverage <- mean(ci$covers)
mcse <- sqrt(coverage * (1 - coverage) / B)
c(coverage = coverage, Monte_Carlo_SE = mcse)
```

Increasing `B` measures coverage more precisely. It does not narrow any
individual study's confidence interval. Increasing `n` changes the study's
information and, typically, its interval width.

## 4. Change the confidence level while holding the sample fixed

For a two-sided interval, split $\alpha$ equally between the two tails.
The positive Normal cutoff has probability $1-\alpha/2$ to its left.

```{r}
levels <- c(.90, .95, .99)
widths <- data.frame(level = levels,
                     estimate = ci$estimate[1],
                     se = ci$se[1]) |>
  mutate(alpha = 1 - level,
         critical = qnorm(1 - alpha / 2),
         lower = estimate - critical * se,
         upper = estimate + critical * se,
         width = upper - lower)
widths

ggplot(widths, aes(y = factor(level), x = estimate)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = lower, xend = upper, yend = factor(level)),
               linewidth = 1.6, color = "#005a8b") +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(x = "Same sample mean and estimated SE", y = "Confidence level")
```

**Try:** add `.80` to `levels` and rerun this chunk. Predict how its width
will compare before looking at the graph.

For a fixed critical value and population SD, the theoretical margin
of error shrinks at rate $1/\sqrt n$:

```{r}
data.frame(n = c(25, 100, 400)) |>
  mutate(SE = sqrt(10) / sqrt(n),
         margin = qnorm(.975) * SE)
```

This last calculation holds the **population** SD fixed; in a real sample,
the estimated SD also varies. More data cannot repair a biased sampling
process merely by producing a smaller SE.

## 5. One statistic, two justifications

Our main argument allows us to estimate the SE. For iid observations with
finite, positive variance,

$$T_n=\frac{\overline X-\mu}{S/\sqrt n}
=\frac{\sigma}{S}\frac{\sqrt n(\overline X-\mu)}{\sigma}
\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1).$$

The CLT gives the Normal limit for the second factor. Consistency of the
sample SD makes the first approach 1. The observations themselves need not
be Normal. This justifies large-sample intervals using an estimated SE.

If we additionally assume iid **Normal** observations, this same statistic
has exactly a $t_{n-1}$ distribution. A $t$ cutoff then supplies exact
finite-sample coverage. We use that special case in the calculation below.

PSD writes $t_{\alpha/2}$ for the **positive upper-tail cutoff**. R uses
left-tail probabilities by default: `qt(1 - alpha/2, df = n - 1)`.

```{r}
set.seed(210)
x <- rnorm(10, mean = 1, sd = sqrt(10))
n <- length(x)
level <- .95
alpha <- 1 - level

se <- sd(x) / sqrt(n)
critical <- qt(1 - alpha / 2, df = n - 1)
manual_ci <- mean(x) + c(-1, 1) * critical * se
manual_ci

# Same positive cutoff, written using the upper tail:
qt(alpha / 2, df = n - 1, lower.tail = FALSE)

# Extract just the confidence interval from t.test's output:
automatic_ci <- t.test(x, conf.level = level)$conf.int
automatic_ci
all.equal(as.numeric(automatic_ci), as.numeric(manual_ci))
```

`$conf.int` selects the interval component of the result. The remaining
`t.test()` output concerns hypothesis testing, which we will develop
separately. The interval concerns the unknown **population mean**; the
sample mean is the number already calculated by `mean(x)`.

### Compare the two reference distributions

```{r}
grid <- data.frame(z = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 1001)) |>
  mutate(normal_density = dnorm(z), t_density = dt(z, df = 9))

ggplot(grid, aes(x = z)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = normal_density, color = "Standard Normal"), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = t_density, color = "t, 9 df"), linewidth = 1, linetype = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Standard Normal" = "#005a8b", "t, 9 df" = "#b34b12")) +
  labs(x = "Standardized sample mean", y = "Density", color = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

c(Normal_cutoff = qnorm(.975), t_cutoff = qt(.975, df = 9))
```

## 6. Why a t cutoff also works asymptotically

For a fixed confidence level, the $t$ critical value approaches the Normal
critical value as its degrees of freedom increase:

```{r}
cutoff_comparison <- data.frame(n = c(10, 30, 100, 500)) |>
  mutate(t_cutoff = qt(.975, df = n - 1),
         normal_cutoff = qnorm(.975))
cutoff_comparison
```

Consequently, under the broad conditions in Section 5, either cutoff gives
asymptotically correct coverage. Choosing a $t$ cutoff does not require us
to claim an exact $t$ distribution for our statistic. In small non-Normal
samples, its larger cutoff still does not guarantee 95% coverage.

### Check the Normal benchmark

The following function compares the two intervals on the **same samples**.
It uses a known Normal population so that the special exact $t$ result
holds. All population parameters are defined inside the function.

```{r}
compare_normal <- function(n, B = 10000) {
  mu <- 1
  sigma <- sqrt(10)
  zcrit <- qnorm(.975)
  tcrit <- qt(.975, df = n - 1)

  stats <- replicate(B, {
    x <- rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
    c(estimate = mean(x), se = sd(x) / sqrt(n))
  })
  z_covers <- abs(stats["estimate", ] - mu) <= zcrit * stats["se", ]
  t_covers <- abs(stats["estimate", ] - mu) <= tcrit * stats["se", ]

  data.frame(n = n, cutoff = c("Normal", "t"),
             critical = c(zcrit, tcrit),
             simulated_coverage = c(mean(z_covers), mean(t_covers)),
             theoretical_coverage = c(2 * pt(zcrit, df = n - 1) - 1, .95))
}

set.seed(2110)
normal_results <- bind_rows(compare_normal(10), compare_normal(500))
normal_results
```

`replicate()` returns a matrix with one column per repetition. The named
rows keep track of each repetition's estimate and SE. The theoretical
Normal-cutoff coverage uses the *actual* $t$ distribution of the statistic:
$P(-1.96\leq T_{n-1}\leq1.96)$, using the unrounded cutoff in the code.

Under this Normal model, at $n=10$ the Normal cutoff gives an interval that
is too narrow too often. At $n=500$, the two critical values and their
coverage are very close. We now check how that conclusion changes with
population shape.

## 7. Check robustness to a skewed population

We now keep the population mean and variance at 1 but change its shape.
A Normal population satisfies the exact $t$ result. An Exponential
population is strongly right-skewed; its $t$ interval is only approximate.

```{r}
coverage_t <- function(n, population, B = 10000) {
  mu <- 1
  critical <- qt(.975, df = n - 1)
  covers <- replicate(B, {
    x <- if (population == "Normal") rnorm(n, 1, 1) else rexp(n, rate = 1)
    margin <- critical * sd(x) / sqrt(n)
    mean(x) - margin <= mu && mu <= mean(x) + margin
  })
  p <- mean(covers)
  c(coverage = p, mcse = sqrt(p * (1 - p) / B))
}

set.seed(2111)
robustness <- expand.grid(n = c(10, 30, 100, 500),
                          population = c("Normal", "Exponential"),
                          stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
robustness$coverage <- NA_real_
robustness$mcse <- NA_real_
for (i in seq_len(nrow(robustness))) {
  result <- coverage_t(robustness$n[i], robustness$population[i])
  robustness$coverage[i] <- result["coverage"]
  robustness$mcse[i] <- result["mcse"]
}
robustness

ggplot(robustness, aes(n, coverage, color = population, linetype = population)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = .95, linetype = 3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .8) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = coverage - 2 * mcse, ymax = coverage + 2 * mcse),
                width = .03) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(10, 30, 100, 500)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Exponential" = "#b34b12", "Normal" = "#005a8b")) +
  labs(x = "Observations per sample (log scale)", y = "Simulated coverage",
       color = "Population", linetype = "Population") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

The whiskers here describe **Monte Carlo uncertainty in estimated coverage**,
not uncertainty in the mean from any single study. Distinguish two questions:

1. How close are the $t$ and Normal critical values?
2. How well does either reference distribution approximate the actual statistic?

The first can be excellent while the second is still poor. The Exponential
population meets our broad asymptotic conditions, but its finite-sample
coverage can fall below 95%. There is no universal sample-size cutoff that
guarantees a good approximation.

## Optional: 100 ratings are not 100 independent voters

Imagine 20 independently sampled voters, each rating a candidate five
times. A voter's ratings share a personal underlying evaluation. We use an
unbounded Normal model for these hypothetical scores to keep the dependence
example transparent.

```{r}
set.seed(2112)
mu <- 50
people <- 20
repeats <- 5
person_mean <- rnorm(people, mean = mu, sd = 10)
ratings <- data.frame(
  voter = rep(seq_len(people), each = repeats),
  rating = rnorm(people * repeats, mean = rep(person_mean, each = repeats), sd = 5)
)

voter_means <- ratings |>
  group_by(voter) |>
  summarise(rating = mean(rating), .groups = "drop")

naive <- t.test(ratings$rating)$conf.int
by_voter <- t.test(voter_means$rating)$conf.int
data.frame(method = c("Treat all 100 rows as independent", "Use 20 voter means"),
           lower = c(naive[1], by_voter[1]),
           upper = c(naive[2], by_voter[2]))
```

With equally many observations per voter, averaging the 20 voter means and
averaging all 100 ratings give the same point estimate. Their SEs differ.

```{r}
set.seed(2113)
B <- 5000
panel_coverage <- replicate(B, {
  person_mean <- rnorm(20, mean = 50, sd = 10)
  ratings <- matrix(rnorm(100, mean = rep(person_mean, each = 5), sd = 5),
                    nrow = 5, ncol = 20)
  # Each column contains one voter's five ratings.
  voter_means <- colMeans(ratings)
  raw_ratings <- as.vector(ratings)
  naive_margin <- qt(.975, 99) * sd(raw_ratings) / sqrt(100)
  voter_margin <- qt(.975, 19) * sd(voter_means) / sqrt(20)
  c(naive = abs(mean(raw_ratings) - 50) <= naive_margin,
    voter_means = abs(mean(voter_means) - 50) <= voter_margin)
})
rowMeans(panel_coverage)
```

This model gives independent Normal voter means, so a $t$ interval on those
means has exact coverage. Averaging within people is appropriate here
because the design is balanced and the target is the mean across voters;
it is not a universal solution for every form of clustered or time-series data.

## Optional: one-sided bounds and the test connection

A lower confidence bound puts the entire error probability in one tail.
Its positive cutoff is `qt(.95, df)` rather than `qt(.975, df)`.

```{r}
set.seed(210)
x <- rnorm(10, mean = 1, sd = sqrt(10))
n <- length(x)
lower_bound <- mean(x) - qt(.95, n - 1) * sd(x) / sqrt(n)
lower_bound
t.test(x, alternative = "greater", conf.level = .95)$conf.int
```

For the corresponding two-sided test, a proposed mean $\mu_0$ falls
outside the 95% interval exactly when its standardized distance exceeds
the two-sided critical value.

```{r}
mu0 <- 0
se <- sd(x) / sqrt(n)
ci95 <- mean(x) + c(-1, 1) * qt(.975, n - 1) * se
outside <- mu0 < ci95[1] || mu0 > ci95[2]
beyond_cutoff <- abs((mean(x) - mu0) / se) > qt(.975, n - 1)
c(outside_interval = outside, beyond_test_cutoff = beyond_cutoff)
```

Choose one-sided versus two-sided inference before examining the result.
A value's presence inside the interval does not prove it is the true mean.
PSD §§8.3–8.4 develop the testing framework; the core demonstration above
only needs confidence intervals and coverage.

## Sources

The main sequence and Normal coverage experiment adapt Matthew Blackwell's
*Gov 2000: Estimation and Statistical Inference*, Section 3, pp. 32–49,
with permission. The $t$ interval and robustness comparisons connect to
[*Probability, Statistics, and Data*, §§8.1–8.5](https://probstatsdata.com/HTCI.html).
The turnout summaries come from Gerber, Green, and Larimer (2008),
“Social Pressure and Voter Turnout: Evidence from a Large-Scale Field
Experiment,” *American Political Science Review*, 102(1), 33–48.
